subject: Five rental questions that require property-specific answers
preheader: Entity structure · partnership terms · property management · first-deal review · refinance math

marketSnapshot.headline: Use a framework, then verify the local answer
marketSnapshot.body: Entity structure, partnership obligations, management termination, acquisition risk, and refinancing all depend on contracts, jurisdiction, financing, insurance, taxes, and the specific property. The examples below are screening questions—not legal, tax, lending, or investment advice.

dealSpotter.address: Q1: Personal title or an entity?
dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Ask lender, insurer, tax adviser, and local counsel
dealSpotter.body: Do not apply a universal property-per-entity formula. Ownership and borrowing choices can affect loan eligibility, insurance, taxes, transfer rules, reporting, costs, and liability. Review the actual financing documents and jurisdiction-specific consequences with qualified advisers before closing or transferring title.

dealSpotter.address: Q2: Who funds an unexpected capital expense?
dealSpotter.body: There is no automatic contribution split that fits every partnership. A reviewed operating or partnership agreement should address contribution requests, reserves, approval authority, defaults, dilution or loans, records, disputes, and exit rights. Have local counsel tailor the language before capital is committed.

dealSpotter.address: Q3: When should a property manager be replaced?
dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Compare contract, evidence, and local requirements
dealSpotter.body: Document service issues, compare leasing and maintenance performance with relevant local evidence, and read the management agreement for notice, termination, records, deposits, and transition duties. Confirm any tenant, trust-account, licensing, or notice obligations locally and line up an orderly handoff before changing managers.

blogFeature.title: Property management yes or no — a comparison framework
blogFeature.excerpt: Compare quoted management costs, leasing terms, maintenance policies, time requirements, and operational risk using the actual agreement rather than a generic percentage claim.

qa.question: Q4: What should I review after a first deal? Q5: How should I screen a refinance?
qa.answer: For an acquisition review, compare the original assumptions with actual closing costs, rent, vacancy, repairs, taxes, insurance, and financing, and record which evidence would improve the next screen. Do not treat an aggressive model as permission to buy. For a refinance screen, compare current and proposed payment schedules, fees, prepayment terms, remaining balance, maturity, cash-out proceeds, reserves, and the expected holding period. A simple fee-divided-by-monthly-savings calculation can be a starting point, but it omits taxes, opportunity cost, changing insurance or escrow, and future financing. Use current written quotes and review lender, tax, and legal consequences with qualified professionals.
